sources.title: The Where, Why, and How of Data Collection
Introduction to Linear Regression and Correlation Analysis
Graphs, Charts, and Tables: Describing Your Data

questions.q: A company computes the average satisfaction score from the customer survey it collected. This is an example of:
questions.e: Simply summarizing/computing a number (the average) from data you already collected is descriptive statistics. Inferential statistics and hypothesis testing go further — they use sample data to draw conclusions or make claims about a larger population, which isn't happening here. "A parameter" is wrong because a parameter is a numerical characteristic of a population (like μ), not a type of statistics — and since the company is only describing its own survey data, it hasn't inferred anything about a wider population.

questions.q: Which data collection method is most likely to suffer from the "Hawthorne Effect"?
questions.e: The Hawthorne Effect is when people change their behavior simply because they know they are being watched — this risk is highest with direct observation, where the researcher is physically present watching subjects in real time. Written questionnaires and telephone surveys ask people to self-report after the fact rather than watching them live, and focus groups are guided discussions, not covert/overt behavioral observation, so the effect is far less of a concern for those methods.

questions.q: A researcher divides a population into strata by income level and takes a simple random sample from each stratum. This is:
questions.e: This is the textbook definition of stratified random sampling: divide the population into meaningful subgroups (strata) and randomly sample from each one. Cluster sampling is different — it randomly selects entire clusters (e.g. whole neighborhoods) and then samples everyone (or randomly) within only the chosen clusters, not from every group. Systematic sampling picks every kth item from a list, and judgment sampling is a nonstatistical method where the researcher hand-picks the sample based on their own judgment — neither involves stratifying by a characteristic like income first.

questions.q: A population has N = 500 and a sample of n = 50 is needed using systematic sampling. What is the sampling interval k?
questions.e: The systematic sampling interval is k = N / n = 500 / 50 = 10 — you pick every 10th item after a random starting point. "5" and "50" come from dividing the wrong numbers together (e.g. 500/100 or just using n alone), and "450" is simply N − n, which is not a meaningful quantity for this formula at all.

questions.q: Temperature measured in degrees Celsius is an example of which data measurement level?
questions.e: Celsius is interval data: the gaps between values are meaningful and consistent (the difference between 10°C and 20°C is the same as between 20°C and 30°C), but 0°C is not a true "absence of temperature" — it's an arbitrary reference point (water's freezing point) — so ratios like "20°C is twice as hot as 10°C" are not meaningful. That absence of a true zero is exactly what rules out "Ratio" (which needs a true zero, like Kelvin). "Nominal" is wrong because Celsius values are ordered numbers, not unordered labels, and "Ordinal" is wrong because the gaps between Celsius values are precisely measurable, not just ranked.

questions.q: Which of the following is a nonstatistical (nonrandom) sampling technique?
questions.e: Convenience sampling means collecting data from whoever is easiest to reach, with no randomization at all — it is the classic nonstatistical (nonrandom/nonprobability) method. Simple random sampling, cluster sampling, and systematic sampling are all statistical (probability) sampling methods, because each one gives every unit in the population a known, calculable chance of being selected.

questions.q: A student's ID number is best classified as:
questions.e: A student ID is nominal data — it's just a unique label used to identify a person; the digits carry no numeric meaning, order, or magnitude (a student with ID 4000012 is not "more" of anything than ID 1000045). That rules out ratio and interval, which both require the numbers to represent measurable quantity, and ordinal, which requires the values to represent a meaningful rank order — an ID number does neither.

questions.q: Explain the difference between sampling error and non-sampling error, and state which one can be reduced by increasing sample size.
questions.m: Sampling error is the unavoidable difference between a sample statistic and the true population parameter that arises simply because a subset (not the whole population) was measured — it exists even with a perfectly executed random sample. Non-sampling error covers all other sources of error: interviewer bias, measurement error, nonresponse bias, poorly worded questions, or data entry mistakes. Increasing the sample size reduces sampling error (though never eliminates it); non-sampling error must be reduced through better procedures and design, not by adding more observations.

questions.q: A company wants to know the average number of hours 10,000 employees spend on training each year. It surveys 200 randomly chosen employees and finds their average is 14.5 hours. Identify the population, the sample, the parameter of interest, and the statistic being computed.
questions.m: Population = all 10,000 employees. Sample = the 200 employees surveyed. Parameter of interest = μ, the true (unknown) average training hours for all 10,000 employees. Statistic = x̄ = 14.5 hours, the average computed from the sample, used as a point estimate of μ.

questions.q: A university wants to survey students but only stops students who happen to be walking by the student center between 12–1pm. Which nonstatistical sampling method is this, and what is the main risk with this approach?
questions.m: This is convenience sampling — data collected in whatever manner is easiest for the researcher. The main risk is that the sample may not represent the full population well (e.g., only students with lunch-time classes near the student center are captured), introducing selection bias into the results.

questions.q: A correlation coefficient of r = -0.91 indicates:
questions.e: r ranges from -1.0 to +1.0, and the magnitude (how close |r| is to 1) tells you the strength of the linear relationship while the sign tells you the direction. |-0.91| = 0.91 is very close to 1, so this is a strong relationship, and the negative sign means x and y move in opposite directions — so it is a strong negative linear relationship. "Weak negative" is wrong because 0.91 is far from 0 (weak would be closer to 0, e.g. -0.15); "strong positive" has the wrong sign; and "no linear relationship" would require r close to 0, not -0.91.

questions.q: Which of the following is true about the least squares method?
o: It minimizes the sum of the residuals (not squared)
It minimizes the sum of the squared residuals, Σ(y - ŷ)²
It minimizes the standard error of the slope only
questions.e: By definition, the least squares method chooses b₀ and b₁ so that Σ(y - ŷ)² (the sum of squared residuals, i.e. SSE) is as small as possible. "Minimizes the sum of the residuals (not squared)" is wrong because the raw (unsquared) residuals from any line through (x̄, ȳ) already sum to zero — that quantity can't be meaningfully minimized further, which is exactly why squaring is needed. "Maximizes r²" describes a side effect (since r² = 1 - SSE/SST, minimizing SSE does raise r²), not the mechanism that defines the method. "Minimizes the standard error of the slope only" is unrelated — the method fits the whole line, not just one coefficient's standard error.

questions.q: In the regression equation ŷ = 175.83 + 49.91x from the Midwest example, what does b₁ = 49.91 mean?
o: 49.91% of sales is explained by years with the company
The correlation between x and y is 49.91
For each additional year with the company, predicted sales rise on average by $49,910
A rep with 0 years of experience is predicted to have $49,910 in sales
questions.e: The slope b₁ is the average change in y for each one-unit increase in x, so b₁ = 49.91 (in thousands of dollars) means predicted sales rise by $49,910 for every additional year with the company. "49.91% explained" confuses the slope with r², which is a percentage; "correlation is 49.91" is impossible since r can only range from -1 to 1; and "0 years → $49,910" describes the intercept b₀ = 175.83, not the slope — a rep with 0 years is predicted to have $175,830 in sales, not $49,910.

questions.q: A regression’s r² = 0.20 means:
o: Only 20% of the variation in y is explained by x; 80% is due to other factors
The model is definitely not useful and should never be reported
80% of the variation in y is explained by x
questions.e: r² = SSR/SST is the proportion of the total variation in y explained by x, so r² = 0.20 means 20% of the variation in y is explained by x, leaving 80% explained by other factors not in the model. "Correlation coefficient is 0.20" confuses r with r² — r would actually be √0.20 ≈ 0.447 here, not 0.20. "Definitely not useful" overstates the case — a low r² means x alone doesn’t explain much of y, but the relationship can still be statistically significant and useful context. "80% explained by x" simply reverses the explained/unexplained percentages.

questions.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes a confidence interval from a prediction interval in regression?
o: They are always exactly the same width
The confidence interval is always wider because it accounts for individual variation
The prediction interval is wider because it must account for the extra variability of a single new observation, not just the mean
The prediction interval only applies when n > 100
questions.e: Compare the two formulas: the CI uses √[1/n + (xₚ-x̄)²/Σ(x-x̄)²] while the PI uses √[1 + 1/n + (xₚ-x̄)²/Σ(x-x̄)²] — the PI has that extra "+1" because it must capture the added uncertainty of one individual y-value scattering around the line, on top of the uncertainty in estimating the mean. That extra term makes the PI strictly wider than the CI at the same xₚ, so "always exactly the same width" and "the CI is always wider" are both backwards, and there is no n > 100 restriction on when a prediction interval applies.

questions.q: A scatter plot shows a clear U-shaped (curvilinear) pattern, but the computed r = 0.05. What should you conclude?
o: There is no relationship between x and y whatsoever
There may be a strong relationship, just not a linear one — r only detects linear association
The data must contain a calculation error
A straight-line regression is still the best model to use here
questions.e: r specifically measures the strength of a straight-line (linear) association — a U-shaped curve can have x and y perfectly related in a nonlinear sense while still producing r ≈ 0, because the positive and negative deviations from a straight line cancel out. So the correct conclusion is that a strong relationship may still exist, just not a linear one. "No relationship whatsoever" ignores the clear pattern visible in the scatter plot; "calculation error" is unwarranted since a low r with a curved pattern is expected, not a sign of a mistake; and fitting a straight line here would still be the wrong model, since the true pattern is curved.

questions.q: Using a regression equation built on x-values ranging from 1 to 9 to predict y at x = 50 is an example of:
questions.e: Extrapolation is using a regression equation to predict y for x-values far outside the range of x actually observed in the sample — here the data only covers x = 1 to 9, so predicting at x = 50 is a large, risky extrapolation with no evidence the linear pattern continues that far. Homoscedasticity refers to residuals having constant variance across x (a model assumption, not a prediction practice); the least squares criterion is the method used to fit the line itself; and the coefficient of determination (r²) measures explained variation, unrelated to the range of x used for prediction.

questions.q: If a regression’s slope t-test gives t = 4.75 with df = 10 at α = 0.05 (two-tailed critical value 2.228), the correct decision is:
o: Fail to reject H₀; the slope could be zero
Reject H₀; the slope is significantly different from zero
The test is inconclusive without the p-value
Recompute using r instead of b₁
questions.e: For a two-tailed test, you reject H₀ when |t| exceeds the critical value. Here |4.75| > 2.228, so H₀: β₁ = 0 is rejected and the slope is judged significantly different from zero. "Fail to reject" is wrong because the computed t clearly exceeds the critical value; the decision is not "inconclusive without the p-value" since comparing t to the critical value is a complete, valid decision rule on its own; and there is no need to "recompute using r" — r and b₁ test the same underlying relationship and are not interchangeable inputs to this test.

questions.q: A sample of n = 8 has Σx = 40, Σy = 200, Σxy = 1,100, Σx² = 220. Compute the slope b₁.
Using the same data as Question 9 (n = 8, x̄ = 5, ȳ = 25, b₁ = 5.0), find the intercept b₀ and the full regression equation.
questions.m: b₀ = ȳ - b₁x̄ = 25 - (5.0)(5) = 25 - 25 = 0. Regression equation: ŷ = 0 + 5.0x, i.e. ŷ = 5.0x.

questions.q: For the Midwest Distribution data (r = 0.8325, n = 12), calculate r² and explain in one sentence what it means about sales.
questions.m: r² = (0.8325)² = 0.6931. About 69.3% of the variation in sales among these reps is explained by how many years they've been with the company; the remaining 30.7% is explained by other factors not in this model.

questions.q: A company wants to know how many of each department's employees (Sales, HR, IT, Finance) work overtime. Which chart is most appropriate?
questions.e: Department is a categorical (qualitative) variable with a handful of distinct, unordered groups, so a bar chart — with a gap between each bar — is the right tool for comparing frequencies across those categories. A histogram is wrong because it's reserved for quantitative data grouped into numeric class intervals with no gaps between bars; a scatter diagram needs two quantitative variables plotted against each other, which doesn't apply here; and an ogive plots cumulative frequency for quantitative data, not categorical counts.

questions.q: A dataset has n = 50 observations. Using the 2^k ≥ n rule, how many classes should you use?
questions.e: You need the smallest integer k such that 2^k ≥ n: 2^5 = 32, which is still less than 50, but 2^6 = 64 ≥ 50, so k = 6 classes. "5" fails the rule because 2^5 = 32 < 50; "7" satisfies the rule (2^7 = 128 ≥ 50) but is not the smallest such k, and the rule always calls for the smallest qualifying value; "50" confuses the number of observations with the number of classes, which defeats the entire purpose of grouping data.

questions.q: The largest value in a dataset is 187 and the smallest is 22. You decide to use 6 classes. What is the class width (before rounding to a "nicer" number)?
questions.e: Class width W = (Largest − Smallest) / Number of classes = (187 − 22) / 6 = 165 / 6 = 27.5. "165" is just the range (187 − 22) before it gets divided by the class count, so it's an intermediate value, not the final width. "20.5" and "30.8" come from dividing 165 by the wrong numbers (e.g. 8 or 5.36) rather than the specified 6 classes.

questions.q: Which statement about histograms and bar charts is TRUE?
o: Both always have gaps between bars.
Histograms have gaps; bar charts do not.
Bar charts have gaps between bars; histograms do not.
questions.e: Bar charts display categorical data, and the gaps between bars visually emphasize that the categories are separate and unordered; histograms display continuous quantitative data grouped into adjoining class intervals, so the bars touch with no gaps to show the data flows continuously from one class into the next. The other three options either reverse this rule or claim both charts behave identically, which contradicts this fundamental (and frequently tested) distinction.

questions.q: A scatter diagram shows points that steadily rise from the lower-left to the upper-right, following a straight-line pattern. This indicates:
questions.e: When points rise from lower-left to upper-right in a straight-line pattern, both variables increase together, which is the definition of a positive linear relationship. A negative linear relationship would instead fall from upper-left to lower-right; "no relationship" would look like a random, patternless scatter of points with no discernible trend; and a curvilinear relationship would bend or curve rather than following a straight line.

questions.q: Which chart is specifically designed to separate the "vital few" categories from the "trivial many," sorting bars from highest to lowest?
questions.e: A Pareto chart is a bar chart sorted in descending order of frequency specifically so the categories responsible for the bulk of a problem (the "vital few") are immediately visible on the left, separating them from the many low-impact categories. A pie chart shows parts of a whole but has no sorting requirement tied to prioritization; an ogive plots cumulative frequency for quantitative data, not categorical ranking; and a stem-and-leaf diagram preserves every individual quantitative value rather than ranking categories by size.

questions.q: In a stem-and-leaf diagram, the value 138 would be split into which stem and leaf?
questions.e: In a stem-and-leaf diagram, the leaf is conventionally the last (rightmost) digit of the value, and the stem is everything before it, so 138 splits into stem = 13 and leaf = 8. "Stem = 1, Leaf = 38" incorrectly treats the leaf as two digits; "Stem = 138, Leaf = 0" invents a leaf digit that isn't part of the original number; and "Stem = 8, Leaf = 13" reverses which part is the stem and which is the leaf.

questions.q: A researcher plots "hours studied" (x-axis) against "exam score" (y-axis) for 40 students. What kind of chart is this, and which variable is dependent?
o: Line chart; hours studied is dependent
Scatter diagram; exam score is dependent
Bar chart; exam score is independent
Pareto chart; hours studied is dependent
questions.e: Plotting two quantitative variables against each other to examine their relationship is exactly what a scatter diagram is for, and by convention the y-axis variable (exam score) is the dependent variable, since it is being examined as a possible outcome of the x-axis variable (hours studied). A line chart is reserved for a single variable tracked over time, not two variables against each other, and it also misidentifies the dependent variable; a bar chart and Pareto chart are for categorical comparisons, not two continuous numeric variables, so neither chart type applies here at all.

questions.q: The following 20 values represent the number of minutes 20 customers waited in line at a bank: 2, 5, 3, 8, 6, 4, 7, 9, 3, 5, 6, 2, 4, 8, 10, 5, 6, 3, 7, 4. Construct a full grouped frequency distribution (using the 2^k ≥ n rule for number of classes, and rounding class width up to a nicer number). Include class limits, frequency, relative frequency, and cumulative frequency.
questions.m: n = 20. Find smallest k with 2^k ≥ 20: 2^4 = 16 (too small), 2^5 = 32 ≥ 20. Use k = 5 classes. Largest value = 10, smallest = 2. W = (10 − 2)/5 = 1.6 → round up to a nicer width, W = 2. Sorted data: 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 5, 6, 6, 6, 7, 7, 8, 8, 9, 10. Resulting table — Class Limits / Frequency / Relative Frequency / Cumulative Frequency: 2–3 / 5 / 0.25 / 5; 4–5 / 6 / 0.30 / 11; 6–7 / 5 / 0.25 / 16; 8–9 / 3 / 0.15 / 19; 10–11 / 1 / 0.05 / 20. Totals: 20 / 1.00.

questions.q: A survey asks 100 shoppers which payment method they used: Cash (35), Credit Card (45), Debit Card (15), Mobile Pay (5). Should this be shown as a pie chart or a bar chart? Justify your answer, and state what percentage each slice/bar would represent.
questions.m: Either works, but a pie chart is especially appropriate here because the four categories are parts of one meaningful whole — all 100 shoppers, no overlaps, covering 100% of the surveyed group. Percentages: Cash = 35/100 = 35%, Credit Card = 45/100 = 45%, Debit Card = 15/100 = 15%, Mobile Pay = 5/100 = 5%. These sum to 100%, confirming a pie chart is valid (unlike a case where the categories do NOT sum to a meaningful total, where a bar chart would be required instead).

questions.q: Explain, using the "vital few vs. trivial many" idea, why a Pareto chart would be more useful than a plain (alphabetically sorted) bar chart for a manager investigating the biggest sources of customer complaints.
questions.m: An alphabetically sorted bar chart forces the reader to scan every bar to figure out which complaint categories matter most. A Pareto chart sorts bars from highest to lowest frequency, so the largest contributors appear first, immediately visible on the left. This lets the manager instantly identify the "vital few" complaint types that account for the majority of the problem (often following something close to an 80/20 pattern) and prioritize fixing those first, rather than spending equal effort across all categories including rare, low-impact ones (the "trivial many").

questions.q: A company has data for ALL of its employees' salaries. Computing the average of this data produces a:
questions.e: Because the data covers ALL employees (the entire population), the average computed from it is a parameter — a numerical summary of a population, usually written μ. "Statistic" and "Sample mean" are wrong because those terms describe a summary computed from only a sample (a subset), not from the full population. "z-score" is wrong because a z-score measures how many standard deviations a single value is from the mean — it is not itself a measure of center.

questions.q: Which measure of center is LEAST affected by an extreme outlier?
questions.e: The median only depends on the position of the middle value(s) in an ordered dataset, so an extreme outlier can only shift which value sits in the middle a little (or not at all) — it does not pull the median toward itself. The mean sums every value including the outlier, so one extreme number can drag it substantially; the weighted mean has this same weakness since it is still built from a sum of the raw values. "Range" is not even a measure of center — it is a measure of spread (max − min), and is in fact extremely sensitive to outliers since it is defined by the extreme values themselves.

questions.q: For a SAMPLE of size n, the sample variance formula divides the sum of squared deviations by:
questions.e: The sample variance formula is s² = Σ(x − x̄)² / (n − 1); dividing by n − 1 (the Bessel correction) rather than n corrects for the fact that a sample tends to underestimate the true population variance, giving an unbiased estimator. "N" and "n" describe the population variance formula (σ² = Σ(x − μ)² / N) or a biased sample estimator — using them on sample data would produce a value that is systematically too small. "n + 1" is not a valid statistical formula at all.

questions.q: A distribution where Mean > Median > Mode is described as:
questions.e: A long right tail of unusually large values pulls the mean upward more than the median, and the median in turn sits above the mode, giving the ordering Mean > Median > Mode — this is the signature of right-skewed (positive) skewness. "Symmetric" is wrong because in a symmetric distribution mean, median, and mode all coincide (or nearly so), not spread apart in an ordered chain. "Left-skewed" would show the opposite order, Mean < Median < Mode, since a long left tail pulls the mean down. "Bimodal" describes a distribution with two peaks/modes, which is a different property entirely and unrelated to this particular ordering.

questions.q: The interquartile range (IQR) is calculated as:
questions.e: IQR = Q3 − Q1 by definition — it is the spread of the middle 50% of the data, from the 75th percentile down to the 25th percentile. "Maximum − Minimum" is the range, a different (and far more outlier-sensitive) measure of spread. "Q2 − Q1" only captures the spread of the second quarter of the data (25th to 50th percentile), and "Q3 − Q2" only captures the third quarter (50th to 75th percentile) — neither spans the full middle 50%.

questions.q: Which rule guarantees a minimum percentage of data within k standard deviations of the mean for ANY distribution shape?
questions.e: Chebyshev's Theorem, at least (1 − 1/k²) of the data lies within k standard deviations of the mean, is proven to hold for ANY distribution shape, no matter how skewed or irregular. The Empirical Rule and the equivalent 68-95-99.7 Rule only apply to bell-shaped (approximately normal) distributions — they give exact approximate percentages (68%, 95%, 99.7%) but are invalid guarantees for skewed or unusual-shaped data. The Bessel Correction is unrelated — it refers to dividing by n − 1 instead of n when computing sample variance, not to a rule about the spread of data around the mean.

questions.q: According to the Empirical Rule, approximately what percentage of bell-shaped data falls within μ ± 2σ?
questions.e: The Empirical Rule states that for bell-shaped (approximately normal) data, about 95% of values fall within 2 standard deviations of the mean (μ ± 2σ). "68%" is the percentage within μ ± 1σ, and "99.7%" is the percentage within μ ± 3σ — both are different k values from this one. "At least 75%" is the Chebyshev's Theorem guarantee for k = 2 (1 − 1/2² = 0.75), which is a weaker, distribution-free lower bound — not the more precise 95% figure that applies specifically to bell-shaped data under the Empirical Rule.

questions.q: The coefficient of variation is most useful for:
o: Finding the middle value of a dataset
Comparing relative variability between datasets with different units or scales
questions.e: CV = (s / x̄) × 100% expresses standard deviation as a percentage of the mean, which strips away the original units — this makes it possible to fairly compare variability between datasets measured in different units or with very different average magnitudes (e.g. grams vs. kilograms, or a machine averaging 250g vs. one averaging 80g). "Finding the middle value" describes the median, "detecting the mode" is a frequency count exercise, and "rounding percentile positions" refers to the index-rounding step used when locating percentiles/quartiles — none of these are what the CV is built for.

questions.q: A data value with a z-score of 2.9 would generally be considered:
o: A moderately unusual value, worth flagging as a possible outlier
Impossible to interpret without the median
questions.e: A z-score of 2.9 means the value sits 2.9 standard deviations from the mean, well past the common outlier-flag threshold of |z| > 2 (and approaching the stricter |z| > 3 threshold), so it is treated as a moderately unusual value worth flagging as a possible outlier. It is not "typical" precisely because most bell-shaped data (per the Empirical Rule) falls within 2 standard deviations of the mean, so 2.9 is far out in the tail. "The mode" is a frequency concept unrelated to z-scores, and z-scores are computed directly from the mean and standard deviation, not the median, so the last option is also incorrect.

questions.q: When computing the weighted mean, the weight w represents:
o: The relative importance assigned to each value of x
questions.e: In x̄w = Σ(wx) / Σw, each weight w scales how much that particular x-value counts toward the average — larger weights mean the value contributes more heavily, reflecting its relative importance (e.g. weighting exam scores by how many points each is worth). Weight is not a measure of spread like standard deviation, not a standardized distance like a z-score, and not a percentile rank — those are separate, unrelated statistics that do not describe "importance" in the weighted-mean sense.

questions.q: Variance is expressed in what kind of units?
o: The same units as the original data
The squared units of the original data
questions.e: Because variance sums squared deviations, (x − x̄)², its units are automatically squared as well — e.g. if the data is in dollars, variance is in dollars². That's exactly why the standard deviation, s = √(s²), exists: taking the square root converts variance back into the same units as the original data, which variance itself is not. "Percentages" describes the coefficient of variation, not variance, and "standard deviations" is a different (related but distinct) statistic, not a unit that variance is measured in.

questions.q: A SAMPLE of 5 exam scores is: 70, 75, 80, 85, 90. Compute the sample mean and sample standard deviation.

Using the running example dataset (starting salaries: 39,000, 44,000, 46,000, 52,000, 56,000, 60,000, 61,000), find Q1, Q3, and the interquartile range. Then determine whether $70,000 would be flagged as an outlier by the 1.5×IQR rule.
questions.m: n = 7. Q1 index = (25/100)(7) = 1.75 → round up to position 2 → Q1 = $44,000. Q3 index = (75/100)(7) = 5.25 → round up to position 6 → Q3 = $60,000. IQR = 60,000 − 44,000 = $16,000. Upper limit = Q3 + 1.5(IQR) = 60,000 + 24,000 = $84,000. Since $70,000 < $84,000, it would NOT be flagged as an outlier — it falls inside the upper limit.

questions.q: Two machines produce parts with the following stats: Machine X has mean weight 250g, standard deviation 12.5g. Machine Y has mean weight 80g, standard deviation 6g. Which machine has more relative variability? Show your work using the coefficient of variation.
questions.m: CV(X) = (12.5/250) × 100% = 5%. CV(Y) = (6/80) × 100% = 7.5%. Even though Machine X has a bigger raw standard deviation (12.5g vs. 6g), Machine Y has the higher coefficient of variation, so Machine Y has more relative variability once its much smaller average weight is accounted for.

questions.q: A process that produces a single outcome whose result cannot be predicted with certainty is called a(n):
questions.e: This is the definition of an experiment — a process (like rolling a die or surveying a customer) whose single result can't be known in advance. "Sample space" is wrong because that's the collection of all possible outcomes of the experiment, not the process itself; "event" is wrong because that's a subset of outcomes you're interested in measuring; and "outcome" is wrong because that's just one single result the experiment could produce, not the process that generates it.

questions.q: Two events are ________ if the occurrence of one precludes the occurrence of the other.
questions.e: Mutually exclusive events cannot happen at the same time — if one occurs, the other is automatically ruled out (e.g., a coin flip can't land both heads and tails). "Independent" is wrong because independence is about one event's occurrence not changing the probability of the other, which is a completely different concept and independent events can still occur together. "Dependent but overlapping" contradicts the very idea of precluding one another, and "complementary" specifically refers to an event and its exact opposite (E and Ē), which is a narrower, distinct relationship from general mutual exclusivity.

questions.q: A weather forecaster says "I believe there is a 70% chance of rain tomorrow" based on years of experience reading patterns, with no formal count of outcomes. Which probability approach is this?
questions.e: This is subjective probability — an assessment based on personal judgment, experience, and available information rather than any calculation. "Classical" requires counting equally likely outcomes from a known sample space (like a die or deck of cards), and "relative frequency" requires an actual historical count of how often rain occurred under similar past conditions — neither is being done here, since the forecaster is relying purely on experience-based belief. "Complement" isn't a probability-assessment approach at all; it's the rule P(Ē) = 1 − P(E).

questions.q: If P(A) = 0.4, P(B) = 0.5, and P(A and B) = 0.2, what is P(A or B)?
questions.e: By the addition rule for any two events, P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B) = 0.4 + 0.5 − 0.2 = 0.7. "0.9" comes from forgetting to subtract the overlap (mistakenly treating A and B as mutually exclusive and using Rule 5 instead of Rule 4). "1.1" comes from adding all three given numbers together (0.4 + 0.5 + 0.2) instead of subtracting the intersection. "0.2" is simply the joint probability P(A and B) itself, confusing it with the union.

questions.q: If P(A) = 0.3, what is P(Ā), the complement of A?
questions.e: The complement rule states P(Ā) = 1 − P(A) = 1 − 0.3 = 0.7. "0.3" wrongly repeats P(A) itself rather than computing its complement. "1.3" comes from adding instead of subtracting (1 + 0.3). "0" is not meaningful here — it would only occur if P(A) were already 1, i.e., a certain event with no complementary probability left over.

questions.q: For independent events E1 and E2, P(E1 and E2) equals:
questions.e: Rule 9, the multiplication rule for independent events, states P(E1 and E2) = P(E1) × P(E2) — since the events don't influence each other, you simply multiply their individual probabilities. "P(E1) + P(E2)" is the (mutually exclusive) addition rule for an "or" question, not an "and" question. "P(E1) × P(E2 | E1)" is Rule 8, the general multiplication rule for any two events (including dependent ones) — it reduces to Rule 9 only because independence means P(E2 | E1) = P(E2), but writing it with the conditional term is the formula for the dependent/general case. "P(E1) − P(E2)" is not a valid probability operation at all.

questions.q: The phrase "given that" in a probability problem is your cue to use:
questions.e: "Given that" restricts the sample space to a specified condition, which is exactly what conditional probability, P(E1 | E2) = P(E1 and E2) / P(E2), is built to handle. The complement rule instead answers "what is the probability this does NOT happen," and the addition rule answers "or" questions about two events — neither restricts the sample space to a condition. "The classical approach only" is wrong because conditional probability can be computed regardless of which probability-assessment approach (classical, relative frequency, or subjective) was used to get the underlying probabilities.

questions.q: A bag has 4 red and 6 blue marbles. One marble is drawn at random. What is the probability it is red?
questions.e: By the classical approach, P(red) = (number of red marbles) / (total marbles) = 4 / 10 = 0.4. "0.6" is actually the probability of drawing blue (6/10), the complement of what was asked. "0.1" would only result from an arithmetic slip such as dividing 1/10 or 4/40. "1.0" would mean certainty, which is wrong since blue marbles are also present.

questions.q: A survey shows 120 of 300 shoppers used a coupon, and of those, 90 purchased. What is P(Purchased | Coupon)?
questions.e: Conditioning on "Coupon" restricts the sample space to the 120 coupon users, of whom 90 purchased: P(Purchased | Coupon) = 90 / 120 = 0.75. "0.30" is the common mistake of dividing the joint cell by the grand total (90/300) instead of by the row total, which actually gives the joint probability P(Purchased and Coupon), not the conditional probability. "0.50" is 150/300, the overall (marginal) probability of purchasing regardless of coupon use — it ignores the "given coupon" condition entirely. "0.90" misreads the numerator 90 as if it were itself the answer, without dividing by anything.

questions.q: Which pair of formulas correctly distinguishes the two addition rules?
o: Rule 4 always subtracts; Rule 5 never subtracts anything at all, ever, for any pair of events
Rule 4 subtracts the intersection (events may overlap); Rule 5 has no intersection term because mutually exclusive events cannot overlap
Rule 4 is for independent events; Rule 5 is for dependent events
Rule 4 uses conditional probability; Rule 5 uses joint probability
questions.e: Rule 4, P(E1 or E2) = P(E1) + P(E2) − P(E1 and E2), applies to any two events and subtracts the intersection so the overlap isn't double-counted; Rule 5, P(E1 or E2) = P(E1) + P(E2), applies only to mutually exclusive events, which by definition cannot both occur, so there is no overlap to subtract. The first option is just an overly-absolute restatement that misses the actual reason (mutual exclusivity, not some blanket rule about "never subtracting"). The third option confuses mutual exclusivity with independence and dependence, which is a completely separate distinction about "and" probabilities, not "or" probabilities. The fourth option is wrong because neither addition rule uses a conditional-probability term or a joint-probability term in isolation — Rule 4 uses a joint probability as the term being subtracted, but that alone doesn't distinguish it the way the option claims.

questions.q: Of 200 employees, a contingency table shows 90 are managers and of those, 30 have an MBA. Overall, 60 employees (managers and non-managers combined) have an MBA. What is P(MBA | Manager)?
questions.m: "Given Manager" restricts our sample space to the 90 managers. Of those, 30 have an MBA. P(MBA | Manager) = 30 / 90 = 1/3 ≈ 0.333.

questions.q: A deck of 52 cards. What is P(King or Spade)?
questions.m: P(King) = 4/52. P(Spade) = 13/52. P(King and Spade) = 1/52 (the King of Spades — don't double count it). P(King or Spade) = 4/52 + 13/52 − 1/52 = 16/52 = 4/13 ≈ 0.308.

questions.q: Two fair coins are tossed. What is the probability of getting at least one head?
questions.m: Use the complement rule. The only way to get zero heads is Tails-Tails: P(TT) = 0.5 × 0.5 = 0.25 (independent tosses, Rule 9). P(at least 1 head) = 1 − P(no heads) = 1 − 0.25 = 0.75.

questions.q: Which of the following is a requirement of a valid discrete probability distribution?
o: 0 ≤ P(x) ≤ 1 for every x, and Σ P(x) = 1
x must be a continuous variable
questions.e: A valid discrete probability distribution requires every individual probability to fall between 0 and 1 inclusive, and the sum of all the probabilities across every possible value of x must equal exactly 1 (100% of the outcomes are accounted for). "Σ P(x) must equal 0" is wrong because probabilities summing to zero would mean no outcome is possible at all. "Every P(x) must be exactly 0.5" confuses one specific case (like a fair coin) with the general rule. "x must be a continuous variable" is backwards — this chapter is specifically about discrete random variables, which take on countable values.

questions.q: A discrete random variable x has E(x) = 40. What does this value represent?
o: The most frequently occurring value of x
The largest possible value of x
The long-run average value of x if the experiment is repeated many times
questions.e: E(x), the expected value, is the mean of the probability distribution — the long-run average outcome you would observe if the random experiment were repeated an enormous number of times, computed as Σ x·P(x). It is not necessarily the most frequent value (that would be the mode) and it is not the largest possible value of x (E(x) is a weighted average, so it can even be a value x never actually takes on). It is also not the standard deviation, which measures spread/variability around E(x), not the average itself.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the four required conditions for a binomial distribution?
o: A fixed number, n, of trials
Only two possible outcomes on each trial
The probability of success changes from trial to trial
questions.e: The four binomial conditions are: a fixed number of trials n, exactly two possible outcomes per trial (success/failure), a constant probability of success p on every trial, and independence between trials. "The probability of success changes from trial to trial" directly contradicts the actual requirement (p must stay constant), which is exactly why it is the one that is NOT a valid condition. The other three answer choices restate real binomial conditions correctly.

questions.q: In the binomial formula P(x) = [n!/(x!(n−x)!)]·pˣ·q^(n−x), what does q represent?
o: The probability of failure, equal to 1 − p
questions.e: q is defined as the probability of failure on a single trial, q = 1 − p, since success and failure are the only two possible outcomes and their probabilities must sum to 1. "The number of trials" is n, "the number of successes" is x, and "the mean of the distribution" is μ = np — none of those is what q stands for in the formula.

questions.q: A binomial experiment has n = 12 and p = 0.30. What is the mean μ?
questions.e: The binomial mean is μ = np = 12 × 0.30 = 3.6. "0.30" is just p by itself, not multiplied by n. "4.0" is a rounding slip (e.g., treating p as roughly 1/3 and doing 12 × 1/3 ≈ 4, or a simple arithmetic mistake), and "12" is just n by itself with no multiplication applied at all.

questions.q: Which scenario is best modeled by a Poisson distribution rather than a binomial distribution?
o: The number of defective items in a batch of exactly 50 inspected units
The number of customer complaints received by a call center per hour
The number of heads in 10 coin flips
The number of job applicants out of 20 who accept an offer
questions.e: Customer complaints "per hour" has no fixed upper bound n — you are counting rare/random occurrences over a continuous interval of time, which is exactly the Poisson setting. The other three all specify a fixed number of trials with two outcomes each (n = 50 inspected units, n = 10 coin flips, n = 20 applicants), which is the defining feature of a binomial experiment, not a Poisson one.

questions.q: In the Poisson formula P(x) = (λt)ˣ·e^(−λt)/x!, what does λ represent?
o: The number of segments of interest
The expected (average) number of successes in one segment
The probability of success on one trial
questions.e: λ is the average (expected) rate of occurrence — the mean number of successes per single segment/interval (e.g., "4 calls per 10 minutes"). It gets multiplied by t, the number of those segments, to scale up to the window you actually care about. Poisson problems have no fixed n or single-trial success probability p at all — those are binomial concepts — so "number of trials" and "probability of success on one trial" don't apply here, and "number of segments of interest" is t, not λ.

questions.q: A call center averages 4 calls every 10 minutes (Poisson). If asked for the probability of receiving exactly 6 calls in a 20-minute period, what value of λt should be used in the formula?
questions.e: λ = 4 calls per 10-minute segment, and the 20-minute window is t = 2 of those segments, so λt = 4 × 2 = 8. Using "4" is the classic mistake of forgetting to scale λ by t and plugging in the raw per-segment rate. "6" is just x (the number of calls asked about), which is a different variable entirely and doesn't belong in λt. "10" has no meaningful derivation from the given numbers.

questions.q: If you are given P(x ≤ 4) = 0.72 from a cumulative binomial table, how would you find P(x ≥ 5)?
o: You cannot find it without more information
questions.e: P(x ≥ 5) is the complement of P(x ≤ 4) since together they cover every possible outcome, so P(x ≥ 5) = 1 − P(x ≤ 4) = 1 − 0.72 = 0.28. Answering "0.72" confuses the event with its complement. "0.72 − 1" flips the subtraction and produces a nonsensical negative probability (−0.28). "You cannot find it without more information" is wrong because the complement rule is exactly the tool needed here — no additional information is required.

questions.q: A discrete random variable has the distribution: P(0) = 0.20, P(1) = 0.50, P(2) = 0.30. Compute E(x) and the standard deviation σ.
A production line has a 10% defect rate (p = 0.10). A sample of n = 6 items is inspected. Use the binomial formula to find the probability that exactly 2 items are defective.
A hospital ER receives an average of 3 patients per 15-minute period (Poisson). Find the probability that exactly 2 patients arrive in a 15-minute period.
questions.m: λ = 3 per 15-minute segment, t = 1, so λt = 3. P(x=2) = 3² · e⁻³ / 2! = 9 · 0.049787 / 2 = 0.4481 / 2. P(x=2) = 0.2240. There is about a 22.4% chance exactly 2 patients arrive in that 15-minute period.

questions.q: In any normal distribution, which three measures of center are always equal?
questions.e: A defining property of the normal distribution is that it is perfectly symmetrical and unimodal, which forces the mean, median, and mode to all fall at the same central point. "Range" and "standard deviation" are measures of spread, not center, so any option pairing them with mode is mixing categories; "variance" is also a spread measure, which rules out the "median, variance, mode" option.

questions.q: The standard normal distribution always has:
questions.e: The standard normal distribution is defined as the specific normal distribution with mean μ = 0 and standard deviation σ = 1 — this is exactly what standardizing (computing z-scores) transforms any normal distribution into. "μ = 100, σ = 15" describes a real but non-standard normal distribution (the IQ scale), not the standard one. Both "μ = 1, σ = 0" and "μ = 0, σ = 0" are impossible for a continuous distribution anyway, since σ = 0 would mean zero spread (every value identical), which cannot produce a bell curve.

questions.q: The correct formula for converting a raw value x to a z-score is:
questions.e: The z-score formula is z = (x − μ) / σ: subtract the mean from the raw value, then divide by the standard deviation, giving the number of standard deviations x is from the mean. "z = (μ − x) / σ" simply flips the sign of the numerator, which would reverse whether a value above the mean reads as positive or negative. "z = x × μ / σ" and "z = (x − σ) / μ" are not meaningful standardization formulas — they mix up which quantity is subtracted and which is divided.

questions.q: If the z-table gives P(0 ≤ Z ≤ 1.50) = 0.4332, what is P(Z > 1.50)?
questions.e: Because the total area to the right of the mean (Z = 0) is exactly 0.5000, the area beyond z = 1.50 is P(Z > 1.50) = 0.5000 − 0.4332 = 0.0668. "0.4332" is just the table value itself, mistakenly used as the final answer without subtracting from 0.5. "0.9332" comes from adding 0.5 + 0.4332 instead of subtracting (that would actually be P(Z < 1.50), the area below 1.50). "0.5668" is an arithmetic slip that doesn't correspond to any valid area in this problem.

questions.q: P(Z < −2.00) equals:
questions.e: The standard normal curve is symmetric about 0, so the area to the left of −2.00 is a mirror image of the area to the right of +2.00: P(Z < −2.00) = P(Z > 2.00). "P(Z < 2.00)" is wrong because that's a much larger area (nearly the whole left side of the curve up to +2.00), not the small tail beyond −2.00. "0.5000" would only be true for P(Z < 0), not P(Z < −2.00). "1 − P(Z > 2.00)" actually equals P(Z < 2.00), not P(Z < −2.00), so it names the wrong complement.

questions.q: A student is finding the score that cuts off the top 5% of a normally distributed exam. What should they search for in the z-table?
o: An area of 0.05 in the table body
An area of 0.45 in the table body
An area of 0.95 in the table body
A z-value of 0.05 in the row/column headers
questions.e: This course's z-table gives the area between the mean and z, P(0 ≤ Z ≤ z) — not the full area to the left of z. If the top 5% is cut off, the area between the mean and the cutoff is 0.50 − 0.05 = 0.45, so the student must search the table body for 0.45. "0.05 in the table body" confuses the tail area itself with the between-mean-and-z area the table actually stores. "0.95 in the table body" would be the answer only if this were a cumulative (left-tail) table, which this one is not. Searching for a "z-value of 0.05" in the headers misunderstands the whole lookup direction — you search areas in the body to find z in the headers, not the reverse.

questions.q: Which of the following is required before you can look up any raw score x in the standard normal table?
o: Nothing — the table accepts raw x-values directly
Converting x into a z-score first
Rounding x to the nearest integer
questions.e: The standard normal table is built entirely in z-units (standard deviations from the mean of 0), so any raw value x must first be standardized via z = (x − μ)/σ before it can be located in the table. It is false that the table accepts raw x-values directly — different distributions have wildly different scales, and the table only works in the universal z-scale. Computing the variance isn't the step that's needed (σ is used directly in the standardizing formula, not σ²), and rounding x to an integer is neither necessary nor part of the standardizing process.

questions.q: The 95% confidence-level critical z-value (two-tailed) is approximately:
questions.e: The standard two-tailed 95% confidence critical value is z = 1.96, one of the four benchmark values (1.28, 1.645, 1.96, 2.575) that recur constantly in this course. "1.28" is the one-tailed 80% cutoff (used for top/bottom-10% percentile problems), "1.645" is the one-tailed 90% cutoff (or two-tailed 90%), and "2.575" is the two-tailed 99% cutoff — each belongs to a different confidence level than the one asked about here.

questions.q: Package weights are normally distributed with μ = 50 kg and σ = 5 kg. Find the probability a randomly chosen package weighs more than 58 kg.
Using the same package-weight distribution (μ = 50, σ = 5), find the probability a package weighs between 45 kg and 55 kg.
questions.m: z1 = (45−50)/5 = −1.00, z2 = (55−50)/5 = 1.00. Since one z is negative and one is positive, the range straddles the mean, so we add both table areas: P(0 ≤ Z ≤ 1.00) = 0.3413 for each side. P(−1.00 < Z < 1.00) = 0.3413 + 0.3413 = 0.6826. (This matches the Empirical Rule: about 68% of values fall within 1 standard deviation of the mean.)

questions.q: Delivery times are normally distributed with μ = 30 minutes and σ = 4 minutes. The company wants to advertise a delivery time such that only 10% of deliveries take longer. What time should they advertise?
questions.m: We want only 10% of area to the right of the cutoff, so 40% of area lies between the mean and the cutoff (0.50 − 0.10 = 0.40). Searching the table body for 0.40 gives z ≈ 1.28. x = μ + z × σ = 30 + (1.28)(4) = 35.12 minutes. The company should advertise a delivery time of about 35 minutes.

questions.q: Sampling error is best described as:
o: A mistake made while entering data
The natural difference between a sample statistic and the true population parameter, caused by which sample happened to be selected
An error caused by a poorly worded survey question
An error that only occurs with small sample sizes
questions.e: Sampling error is the unavoidable gap between a sample statistic (x̄ or p̄) and the true population parameter (μ or p) that exists purely because a subset — not the entire population — was measured; it happens with every random sample, even a perfectly executed one. Data entry mistakes and poorly worded questions are examples of non-sampling error, which is avoidable through better procedures, not an inherent property of sampling itself. It is also wrong to say this only happens with small samples — sampling error shrinks as n grows (via σ/√n) but never disappears entirely, even for large samples.

questions.q: According to the Central Limit Theorem, as the sample size n increases, the sampling distribution of x̄:
o: Stays exactly the same shape as the population
Becomes approximately normal, regardless of the population’s shape
questions.e: This is the core statement of the Central Limit Theorem: no matter what shape the underlying population has (even skewed or non-normal), the sampling distribution of x̄ approaches a normal shape as n gets larger. "Stays exactly the same shape as the population" describes what would happen without the CLT at all — the whole point of the theorem is that the sampling distribution normalizes even when the population does not. "Becomes more skewed" is the opposite of what actually happens, since averaging over more observations smooths out skewness rather than amplifying it.

questions.q: What is the standard error of the sample mean, σ_x̄?
questions.e: The standard error of the mean is defined as σ_x̄ = σ/√n — the population standard deviation shrunk by the square root of the sample size, reflecting that averages vary less than individual observations. "σ" alone ignores sample size entirely and is just the population standard deviation. "σ × √n" has the relationship backwards (it would make the standard error grow with n, which is wrong — larger samples should give more precise, not less precise, estimates). "σ / n" over-shrinks the value by dividing by n instead of √n, a common arithmetic slip.

questions.q: A population has σ = 20 and a sample of n = 25 is taken. What is the standard error of the mean?
questions.e: σ_x̄ = σ/√n = 20/√25 = 20/5 = 4. "20" is just the raw population σ with no adjustment for sample size at all. "0.8" comes from dividing by n instead of √n (20/25 = 0.8), a classic mix-up of the standard error formula. "500" comes from multiplying instead of dividing (20 × 25), which has no basis in the formula at all.

questions.q: The conservative rule-of-thumb sample size needed for the Central Limit Theorem to guarantee an approximately normal sampling distribution, regardless of population shape, is:
questions.e: The standard conservative rule of thumb taught for the CLT is n ≥ 30 — once the sample size reaches about 30, the sampling distribution of x̄ can be treated as approximately normal even if the population itself is not normal. "n ≥ 5" and "n ≥ 10" are both far too small to guarantee normality for a noticeably skewed population — those thresholds are commonly confused with the np ≥ 5 / nq ≥ 5 conditions used for proportions, not the CLT rule for means. "n ≥ 100" is unnecessarily conservative; textbooks do not require that large a sample for the CLT approximation to kick in.

questions.q: A student computes z = (x̄ − μ)/σ (without dividing by √n) for a sample-mean problem. What is wrong with this calculation?
o: The denominator should be the standard error σ/√n, not the raw population standard deviation σ
The numerator should be μ − x̄ instead
z-scores cannot be used for sample means
questions.e: When standardizing a sample mean, the denominator must be the standard error of the mean, σ/√n, not the raw population σ — using σ alone treats the sample mean as if it were a single raw observation, which understates how tightly x̄ clusters around μ and produces a z-score that is too small in magnitude. The numerator x̄ − μ is already correctly ordered (using μ − x̄ would just flip the sign, which is not "the" problem here). z-scores absolutely can and are routinely used for sample means — that option is simply false.

questions.q: Which conditions must hold for the sampling distribution of a sample proportion p̄ to be approximately normal?
o: The population must already be normal
questions.e: For proportions, normality of the sampling distribution of p̄ is checked with np ≥ 5 and nq ≥ 5 (where q = 1 − p) — both the expected number of successes and failures must be reasonably large. "n ≥ 30 only" is the rule of thumb for the sampling distribution of the mean (CLT), not for proportions, so applying it here is a common mix-up between the two chapters’ conditions. "p = 0.5 exactly" is not required — np ≥ 5 and nq ≥ 5 can hold for many values of p, not just 0.5. "The population must already be normal" is irrelevant for proportions, since the underlying variable is binary (success/failure), not a continuous normal quantity.

questions.q: What is the standard error of a sample proportion, σ_p̄?
questions.e: The standard error of the sample proportion is σ_p̄ = √( p(1 − p) / n ) — the variance of a proportion is p(1−p)/n, so taking the square root gives the standard error, mirroring how σ/√n works for the mean. "p(1 − p)" is only the variance term without dividing by n or taking the square root. "√p / n" and "p / √n" both scramble the formula by taking the square root of, or dividing by √n, the wrong piece (p alone) instead of applying √ to the entire p(1−p)/n expression.

questions.q: A problem states "60 out of 150 sampled customers preferred Brand A." Which sampling distribution applies, and what is p̄?
o: Sampling distribution of the mean; x̄ = 60
Sampling distribution of a proportion; p̄ = 60/150 = 0.40
Sampling distribution of the mean; x̄ = 0.40
questions.e: This is a yes/no, success/failure situation (preferred Brand A or not), which is exactly what the sampling distribution of a proportion is built for; p̄ = x/n = 60/150 = 0.40. The two "mean" options misapply the wrong sampling distribution to a categorical count — the raw count 60 is not itself a sample mean, and even after correctly computing 0.40, that value is a proportion, not an x̄. Nothing here is ambiguous or missing, so "cannot be determined" is incorrect — both the count (60) and the sample size (150) needed to compute p̄ are given.

questions.q: A population of delivery times is normally distributed with μ = 30 minutes and σ = 8 minutes. Find the probability that the mean delivery time of a random sample of n = 16 deliveries is greater than 33 minutes.
questions.m: σ_x̄ = σ/√n = 8/√16 = 8/4 = 2. z = (33 − 30)/2 = 1.50. P(0 ≤ z ≤ 1.50) = 0.4332 (from standard normal table). P(z > 1.50) = 0.5000 − 0.4332 = 0.0668. There is about a 6.68% chance the sample mean delivery time exceeds 33 minutes.

questions.q: A machine fills bottles with a mean of μ = 500 mL and σ = 12 mL (population approximately normal). Find P(x̄ < 495) for a sample of n = 36 bottles.
questions.m: σ_x̄ = 12/√36 = 12/6 = 2. z = (495 − 500)/2 = −2.50. P(0 ≥ z ≥ −2.50) = 0.4938. P(z < −2.50) = 0.5000 − 0.4938 = 0.0062. Only about a 0.62% chance the sample mean fill is below 495 mL — this would be a red flag for the filling process.

questions.q: A polling firm believes 45% of voters (p = 0.45) support a proposition. In a random sample of n = 120 voters, what is the probability that the sample proportion p̄ is between 0.40 and 0.50?
A single statistic, such as x̄, used to estimate an unknown population parameter is called a:
questions.e: A point estimate is exactly this — a single sample statistic (like x̄ or p̄) used as a best guess for the unknown population parameter. A confidence interval is a range built around the point estimate, not the point estimate itself. The margin of error is the ± amount added to the point estimate to build that interval, and the critical value (z) is the multiplier used to compute the margin of error — neither of those is itself "a single statistic used to estimate a parameter."

questions.q: What is the correct critical value (z) for a 99% confidence interval?
questions.e: For a 99% confidence level, α = 0.01, so α/2 = 0.005 is left in each tail, and the z-value that leaves 0.005 in the upper tail is z = 2.575. 1.28 corresponds to 80% confidence, 1.645 corresponds to 90% confidence, and 1.96 corresponds to 95% confidence — each pairs with a smaller confidence level, so all three leave too much area in the tails for a 99% interval.

questions.q: If the confidence level is increased from 90% to 99% while the sample size stays the same, the margin of error will:
questions.e: Moving from 90% to 99% confidence increases the critical value z from 1.645 to 2.575, and since the margin of error e = z(σ/√n) is directly proportional to z, a larger z produces a larger margin of error — the interval must widen to be more confident of capturing μ. It cannot "decrease" or "stay the same" because z genuinely changes when confidence changes (with n and σ fixed), and a margin of error is always a positive quantity, so "become negative" isn't possible.

questions.q: A sample of n = 100 accounts has x̄ = $2,000 and σ = $400. What is the margin of error for a 95% confidence interval?
questions.e: Margin of error e = z(σ/√n) = 1.96 × (400/√100) = 1.96 × (400/10) = 1.96 × 40 = $78.40. "$40.00" is just σ/√n with the z-multiplier left out, "$400.00" is simply σ itself (never divided by √n or multiplied by z), and "$1.96" is just the critical value written as if it were a dollar amount rather than a multiplier.

questions.q: A researcher wants a margin of error of e = 5 with 95% confidence, and estimates σ = 25. What sample size is required? (n = (zσ/e)², round up)
questions.e: n = (zσ/e)² = (1.96 × 25 / 5)² = (49/5)² = 9.8² = 96.04, which rounds up to n = 97 — sample size is always rounded up so the target margin of error is not missed. "n = 24" and "n = 49" are far too small (they look like the square root step, or 49/... , was skipped or mishandled), and "n = 125" overshoots by using an incorrect intermediate value; only 97 satisfies the formula with these exact inputs.

questions.q: In the formula for the confidence interval of a proportion, p̄(1 − p̄)/n plays the same role that which quantity plays in the mean formula?
questions.e: The standard error of the mean is σ/√n, so the variance-of-the-estimator term underneath the square root is σ²/n; the standard error of a proportion is √(p̄(1−p̄)/n), so its variance-of-the-estimator term is p̄(1−p̄)/n — p̄(1−p̄) is simply standing in for σ² as the measure of variability. "z²" is unrelated (z is the critical value, not a variance term), "x̄" is the point estimate for the mean (parallel to p̄, not to p̄(1−p̄)/n), and "the margin of error e" is the final ± amount (z times the standard error), not the variance term inside the square root.

questions.q: Which statement about a "95% confidence interval" is correct?
o: There is a 95% probability that μ falls inside this specific interval.
If many such intervals were constructed from repeated samples, about 95% of them would contain the true μ.
95% of the population's data values fall inside this interval.
The sample mean equals μ with 95% certainty.
questions.e: Confidence level is a long-run frequency statement about the procedure, not a probability statement about one already-computed interval: once a specific interval is calculated, μ either is or is not in it — the 95% describes that if you repeated the sampling process many times, about 95% of the resulting intervals would capture the true μ. The first option misapplies probability language to a fixed interval, the third confuses a confidence interval about the parameter μ with a range statement about individual data values, and the fourth is wrong because x̄ is a single point estimate that essentially never exactly equals μ, let alone "with 95% certainty."

questions.q: Explain why increasing the confidence level widens a confidence interval, while increasing the sample size narrows it. Use the formula x̄ ± z(σ/√n) in your answer.
questions.m: Increasing the confidence level requires a larger critical value z (e.g., 1.645 → 1.96 → 2.575 as confidence rises from 90% to 95% to 99%), which directly increases the margin of error z(σ/√n) and widens the interval — you need a "wider net" to catch μ more often. Increasing the sample size n makes the denominator √n larger, which shrinks the standard error σ/√n and therefore shrinks the margin of error, narrowing the interval — more data means less sampling variability, so the point estimate becomes more precise.

questions.q: A survey of 400 customers finds that 60 are dissatisfied with a product. Construct and interpret a 90% confidence interval for the true proportion of dissatisfied customers.
questions.m: p̄ = 60/400 = 0.15. Standard error = √(0.15 × 0.85/400) = √(0.1275/400) = √0.00031875 ≈ 0.01785. Margin of error = z × SE = 1.645 × 0.01785 ≈ 0.02937. Confidence interval = 0.15 ± 0.0294 → [0.1206, 0.1794], i.e., about 12.1% to 17.9%. Interpretation: with 90% confidence, the true proportion of dissatisfied customers is between about 12.1% and 17.9%.

questions.q: A researcher wants to estimate a population proportion with a margin of error of e = 0.03 at 95% confidence, and has no prior estimate of p̄. What sample size should be used, and why is p̄ = 0.5 chosen in this situation?
questions.m: Using n = p̄(1−p̄)(z/e)² with p̄ = 0.5: n = 0.5 × 0.5 × (1.96/0.03)² = 0.25 × (65.33)² = 0.25 × 4268.4 ≈ 1067.1 → round up to n = 1068. p̄ = 0.5 is chosen because p̄(1−p̄) is maximized when p̄ = 0.5 (0.5 × 0.5 = 0.25, the largest possible value of that product), which gives the most conservative — i.e., the largest — required sample size. This guarantees the margin of error target is met no matter what the true p̄ later turns out to be.
